items.title: I Built a LeetCode for Practicing System Design
items.author: Ashish Pratap Singh
items.content:
Excited to share new practice resources at to help you go beyond theory and actually implement concepts from system design, low-level design, and concurrency.

Many of the problems are free to practice. For full access and unlimited submissions, you can subscribe to .

Each problem includes a clear description, input/output examples, hints, starter code, and multiple test cases to validate your solution.

Supported languages include: Java, Python, C++, C# and Go.

Once you submit your code, you can also use AI-powered code review to identify potential issues and get suggestions for improving your implementation.

The problems are connected directly to the relevant sections inside our learning resources, so you can learn a concept and immediately practice implementing it:

The goal is to make the learning process more hands-on. Instead of only reading about concepts such as rate limiting, caching, design patterns, thread safety, or synchronization, you can now implement them and test whether your solution actually works.

If you want to see how DSA concepts are actually used in real-world systems, going through system design exercises is a great way to connect theory with practical applications.

If you want to get better at turning requirements into clean, maintainable code, low-level design exercises are a great way to practice object-oriented design, design patterns, and structuring real-world applications.

If you want to understand how multithreaded systems actually work, concurrency exercises are a great way to practice concepts like synchronization, locks, race conditions, and thread safety through real implementations.

This feature is still new and experimental, and I’ll continue improving the problem quality, test cases, evaluation, and overall practice experience.

If you try it out, please let us know if you have any suggestions or feedback. It will help us make the experience better.

Here, you work through an interview problem step by step in a realistic interview setting. The AI interviewer asks follow-up questions, challenges your decisions, and provides detailed feedback on your performance.

Together, the learning resources, implementation problems, and mock interviews are designed to help you move through the full interview-preparation loop:

Learn the concept → implement it → practice explaining your decisions in an interview.

Thank you for all the support, and I hope you find these new resources useful.

items.title: Real-Time Communication Patterns for System Design Interviews
items.author: Ashish Pratap Singh
items.content:
When systems need to receive updates as soon as they happen, there are four common approaches: , , , and .

They all solve a similar problem: delivering new information without waiting for the next normal request. But they do it in very different ways, and each is better suited to a different communication pattern.

In this article we’ll look at how each one works, its trade-offs, and when to use it.

I also created a on real-time communication patterns with visuals and animations.

Subscribe for more such videos!

Traditional HTTP is client-driven. The client sends a request, and the server responds. The server does not send anything unless the client asks first.

So if the client wants fresh data, one simple option is to the server every few seconds:

That works when updates are infrequent, or when a small delay is acceptable.

But real-time applications are different. Updates can happen at any moment, and the client does not know when they will arrive. That creates a trade-off:

  • , and users see delays. If a new message arrives just after a poll, the client has to wait until the next one.

  • , and you waste resources on requests that often return no new data.

Real-time systems need a more efficient way to receive updates as soon as they become available. Each of the four approaches below solve this problem in a different way.

Long Polling works on top of regular HTTP. The main difference is that the server does not always respond right away.

Suppose a client wants to know when a new message arrives. It sends a request to the server.

  • , the server responds immediately.

  • , the server does not return an empty response. It keeps the request open and waits.

When a new message arrives, the server sends it as the response. The client then immediately opens another request and waits again.

This creates an almost continuous flow of updates, even though each update still uses a separate HTTP request.

The biggest advantage of Long Polling is . It uses standard HTTP, so it works with existing browsers, proxies, and load balancers. There is no new protocol to support.

The downside is overhead.

  • Every update costs a full request. After each response, the client sends a new request with headers, authentication data, and other metadata. For a small update, that metadata can be larger than the data itself.

  • The server has to keep a request open for every waiting client. At small scale this is fine. With hundreds of thousands of clients, the cost adds up.

  • There is a gap between requests. Between one response and the next request, the client is not listening. An update that arrives in that gap is delayed, and it can be missed entirely if the server does not track what each client has already seen.

The usual fix for that last problem is a cursor. The client sends the ID of the last event it received, and the server returns everything after it before it starts waiting.

So Long Polling is simple and practical, but it is less efficient for high-frequency updates.

Server-Sent Events also use HTTP. But unlike Long Polling, the connection stays open after an update is sent.

The client opens one connection, and the server keeps sending new events over it. The client never has to create a new request after each update.

On the wire, SSE uses a simple text-based format. Each event is sent as one or more fields such as and , followed by a blank line:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream

id: 41
data: {"type": "notification", "text": "Build finished"}

id: 42
data: {"type": "notification", "text": "New comment on your PR"}

A common modern use case of SSE is streaming responses from large language models. Instead of waiting for the entire answer to be generated, the server sends chunks of the response as they become available, all over the same open connection.

This makes SSE more efficient than Long Polling for continuous server-to-client updates.

Browsers support SSE natively through the API, and it reconnects on its own if the connection drops:

const events = new EventSource('/events');

events.onmessage = (event) => {
  showNotification(JSON.parse(event.data));
};

If the server tags events with an , the browser sends the last one it saw in a header when it reconnects. The server can then resume from that point instead of starting over.

The most important thing to understand about SSE is that it only flows . The client cannot send messages back over the same connection. If it needs to send something, it makes a separate HTTP request.

That makes SSE a good fit when communication mainly flows in one direction:

  • Progress updates for long-running jobs

But what if both the client and the server need to send data to each other in real time? That is where WebSockets come in.

WebSockets are designed for persistent, two-way communication between a client and a server.

The connection usually starts as a normal HTTP request. The client asks the server to upgrade the connection to the WebSocket protocol:

GET /game HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

If the server accepts, it replies with . From then on, the connection stays open and both sides can send messages at any time.

After the upgrade, data no longer travels as HTTP requests and responses. It travels as lightweight , which carry only a few bytes of framing instead of a full set of HTTP headers.

Example: A Multiplayer Game

Suppose we are building a multiplayer game.

  1. When a player moves, their client immediately sends that update to the server.

  2. The server pushes the new position to every other player over their existing WebSocket connections.

  3. Nobody has to ask the server whether anything changed.

Because the connection is bidirectional, each client keeps sending its own actions while it receives everyone else’s in real time.

When WebSockets Make Sense

WebSockets are a natural fit when both sides need to communicate frequently, in real time, with low latency. Common examples include:

  • Other highly interactive applications, such as live trading screens

The Cost: Operational Complexity

WebSockets are powerful, but that power comes with more operational complexity.

Every connected user keeps a connection open. At scale, that can mean hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of active connections spread across many servers.

Suppose a user is connected to server A, but an event for that user is generated on server B. Server B cannot send the event directly to the client. It first needs to get that event to server A, which owns the connection.

This usually requires shared infrastructure such as a message broker or pub/sub system that lets WebSocket servers exchange events.

Connections will eventually drop. Clients need reconnection logic, servers need to detect dead connections, and deployments need a graceful way to drain existing connections before shutting a server down.

So WebSockets are a strong choice for true two-way, low-latency communication, but they are also the most operationally demanding of the four approaches to run at scale.

So far, every approach has focused on communication between a client and a server. But real-time events also happen , where one service needs to notify another when something happens.

In these cases, keeping a persistent connection open is often unnecessary. That is where come in.

Suppose your application uses a payment provider like Stripe. A customer starts a payment, but it may take several seconds, or even minutes, to complete.

Your backend could keep polling the provider to ask whether the payment has finished. But that wastes requests, and the answer is “no” most of the time.

Instead, your application gives the payment provider an , such as . When the payment succeeds, the provider sends an HTTP request to that endpoint with the payment details:

POST /webhooks/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Webhook-Signature: t=1758700000,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e7

{"id": "evt_1042", "type": "payment.succeeded", "order_id": "ord_881", "amount": 4900}

Your server receives the request, reads the event, processes it, and returns .

The key difference from SSE and WebSockets is that there is no persistent connection. When an event occurs, the sender makes a normal HTTP request to the receiver. Once the request is handled, the connection can close.

This makes Webhooks a good fit for events that happen occasionally and at unpredictable times, such as:

  • Code is pushed to a repository and CI should run

  • An email is delivered or bounces

  • A file finishes processing

Webhooks sound simple, but reliable delivery needs a few extra considerations.

Your server might be down, slow, or return an error when the webhook arrives. The sender should not assume the event was processed. Webhook providers usually retry failed deliveries, often with increasing delays between attempts.

Retries create a new problem: the same event can arrive more than once. For example, your server processes the payment, but its is lost on the way back. The provider sees a failure and sends the event again.

That means handlers should be . Record each event ID you process, and skip any event you have already seen, so a duplicate does not mark an order as paid twice or trigger a second shipment.

async function handlePaymentWebhook(event) {
  // Skip events we have already processed
  if (await processedEvents.has(event.id)) return;

  await markOrderPaid(event.order_id);
  await processedEvents.add(event.id);
}

In production, the check and the write should happen in one transaction, or behind a unique constraint on the event ID, so two copies arriving at the same time cannot both get through.

Because a webhook endpoint is exposed to the internet, anyone can try to send requests to it. Your server therefore needs a way to verify that each request actually came from the expected sender.

A common solution is . The sender and receiver share a secret key. The sender uses that secret to compute an HMAC over the request payload and includes the signature in a header.

When the webhook arrives, the receiver computes the HMAC again using the same secret and compares the two signatures. If they do not match, the request is rejected.

Many systems also include a timestamp in the signed data. This allows the receiver to reject old requests and helps protect against replay attacks, where someone captures a valid webhook and sends it again later.

If you want to go deeper into these topics like how to make Webhooks reliable or how to scale WebSockets across millions of connections, I cover them in much more detail in my resource at .

It includes visual explanations, animations, quizzes, and hands-on exercises to help you apply these concepts in real system design scenarios.
